Romanian Leu Plunges Amid Currency Crisis, Businesses and Consumers Struggle

Romania is facing its most severe currency crisis in decades as the leu slumps to historic lows against the euro and dollar, igniting widespread economic turmoil. The National Bank of Romania’s emergency measures have failed to stem the slide, and inflation is accelerating rapidly, with the annual rate now estimated at 28%, according to the Romanian Institute for Economic Research.

This week, the leu fell to 6.05 against the euro, down 19% since the start of the year. The depreciation has prompted sharp price increases for imported goods and fuel, putting pressure on both businesses and households. “We’ve had to raise prices twice in the last three months just to cover our costs,” said Andrei Popescu, CEO of food retailer Alimentar Plus. “Customers are buying less, and suppliers are demanding payment in euros.”

The government has called for calm and pledged to protect the most vulnerable. “We are working closely with the central bank and international partners to stabilize the currency and ensure essential imports continue,” Finance Minister Ioana Rădulescu said at a press briefing. However, the government’s ability to intervene is limited by growing fiscal deficits and a declining pool of foreign currency reserves, which have dropped to €26 billion, down from €34 billion at the start of the year.

Small manufacturers and exporters are feeling the strain. “We import machinery and raw materials in euros, but our sales are mostly in lei,” said Marius Ionescu, owner of textile producer RomTextil. “Our margins have evaporated.”

Unions report a surge in requests for wage increases. “Workers are struggling to afford basic necessities as prices rise,” said Anca Marinescu, spokesperson for the National Union of Industrial Employees.

Analysts warn that without external assistance, the leu could weaken further. “Romania needs a credible plan and potentially a support package from the IMF or EU,” said economist Vlad Petrescu of East Europe Financial Advisors.

The currency crisis has already slowed economic activity. The National Institute of Statistics reported a 2.1% contraction in GDP for the first quarter, with further declines expected if the crisis persists.
